newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sluggish chip market haunts Japan electronic firms.
newsitem.headline: Sluggish chip market haunts Japan electronic firms.

text.p: Tumbling chip prices have cast a cloud over Japanese electronics firms' interim earnings, but robust sales of communications products helped make their overall business performance look less gloomy.

Faced with sluggish prices for 16-megabit dynamic random access memory chips (DRAMs), most chip makers revised down semiconductor investment plans and looked into other niche products, such as micro controller unit (MCU) chips used for household electronic devices.

NEC Corp said its parent profit rose 31.6 percent to 40.16 billion yen ($355 million) in the six months to September 30, after brisk telecommunications business eased the pain from slumping semiconductor operations.
For the year to March 31, 1997, NEC forecast current profit of 105 billion yen ($929 million), up 4.4 percent.
Current profit is pretax and includes gains or losses on non-operating activities, such as investment in stocks.
"In the electronics industry, domestic telecommunications saw continuing demand for mobile communications systems, switching systems and transmission systems," NEC said.
But it added in a statement: "The semiconductor field...experienced a very different situation due to dropping memory prices."
NEC and four other major chip manufacturers -- Toshiba Corp, Hitachi Ltd, Fujitsu Ltd and Mitsubishi Electric Corp -- were still haunted by worries over sagging semiconductor chip prices.
The five revised down their semiconductor investment plans by 75 billion yen ($663 million) to a total of 815 billion yen ($7.21 billion) for the current fiscal year.

Amid a supply glut following a worldwide slowdown in personal computer sales, prices of 16-megabit DRAMs -- the current mainstay products used in PCs -- nosedived more than 70 percent over the past 10 months.
The price falls appeared to have halted in early October after makers curtailed supplies, but few manufacturers believe they have put the worst behind them.

Of the five, Hitachi appears to have been hit hardest. It suffered a 51.3 percent drop in its current profit to 26.74 billion yen ($236 million) for the half-year, followed by Mitsubishi Electric, which posted a 35.8 percent fall in its interim profit to 24.04 billion yen ($212 million).

Hitachi forecast a profit slump by 45.7 percent to 70 billion yen ($619 million) for the full year, while Mitsubishi forecast a 30.6 percent drop in its full-year profit to 70 billion yen ($619 million).
"We expect the memory chip business to remain tough for the next two business years," a Hitachi spokesman said.
He said chip makers' production would shift into the next-generation 64-megabit DRAMs late next year, but Hitachi expected this business would also be very tough.

While reducing chip investment, Hitachi is also trying to increase production output of MCU chips and concentrate less on memory chips for personal computers. This fiscal year, memory chips account for 40 percent of its semiconductor business, and it is trying to reduce this ratio, he added.
Toshiba also remained pessimistic, saying a full recovery of the chip market was unlikely until the end of 1997.
It posted a healthy 48.8 percent jump in its interim profit to 48.11 billion yen ($425 million), but forecast only a scant 3.0 percent increase for the full year.

"As we expect expansion in production capacity by semiconductor makers, including Taiwanese makers, to continue next year, a profit recovery in the chip industry is unlikely next year," Toshiba Vice President Atsumi Uchiyama told a news conference.
"In terms of sagging profit in semiconductor business, the situation will be harder in the latter half of this year than the first half," he said.
